title: Variantscape: Retrospective Study of Large Language Model-Based Extraction of Variant-Treatment-Cancer Associations from Published Oncology Abstracts
authors: Wosny, M.; Blindu, A. S.; Boesch, M.; Peres, T.; Niederhauser, T.; Fruh, M.; Rothermundt, C.; Hastings, J.
abstract: ObjectivesPrecision oncology relies on accurate interpretation of tumour-detected gene variants, to guide personalised treatment decisions. However, interpretation of variants in context requires extensive information that is often buried within unstructured biomedical literature and obscured by inconsistent nomenclature, making manual retrieval labour-intensive and prone to omissions. In this study, our aim was to evaluate the potential of large language models to extract variant-treatment-cancer associations at scale from published abstracts. DesignWe developed Variantscape, a large-scale, automated pipeline and open-access web tool. It integrates traditional natural language processing methods with state-of-the-art large language models to extract, standardise, and analyse co-associations between genetic variants, cancer types, and therapeutic interventions from published biomedical abstracts. ResultsFrom over 3.7 million abstracts published between January 2014 and October 2026, 886,195 articles containing gene names were eligible for extraction. Among these, 37,895 (4.3%) mentioned a variant, cancer type, and therapeutic agent together, covering 11,985 unique variants across 197 cancer types and 547 therapeutic agents. LLM verification against the abstract text confirmed at least one association in 35,224 papers, giving a literature-derived graph of 10,571 nodes and 44,644 verified edges. Canonical alterations in well-studied cancers (e.g., BRAF V600E in melanoma) were strongly linked to established treatments, while several rare variants also emerged with high-confidence literature support. ConclusionsBy applying large language models to biomedical literature, Variantscape enables scalable, context-aware extraction of trilateral variant-treatment-cancer relationships. This approach supports early evidence synthesis/hypothesis generation, highlights underrecognized or rare associations for MTB preparation, and offers a practical resource for accelerating discovery and supporting precision oncology research and translation. FundingThis study was funded by the School of Medicine at the University of St. Gallen in Switzerland under grant number 2300380. Article SummaryO_ST_ABSStrengths and limitations of this studyC_ST_ABS[bullet] Variantscape combines traditional natural language processing with large language models to enable scalable, automated extraction of variant-cancer-treatment relationships from over 3.7 million biomedical abstracts, substantially reducing the manual search burden inherent to existing molecular tumour board workflows. [bullet]The pipeline applies large language model-based inference to standardise inconsistent genetic nomenclature across the literature, improving the comparability and reliability of extracted associations that would otherwise be obscured by terminological variation. [bullet]Variantscape is designed as a continuously updatable, open-access resource, meaning it can incorporate newly published evidence without requiring repeated manual intervention. [bullet]The pipeline relies solely on abstract-level text rather than full-text articles, which may limit the depth and granularity of extracted associations, as key methodological details, variant context, and nuanced clinical findings are frequently reported only within the body of published papers. [bullet]Automated extraction using large language models introduces a risk of misattribution of variant-cancer-treatment relationships, and without systematic manual validation of outputs, the precision of identified associations at scale remains difficult to fully characterise.

infographic.key_insight: Variantscape uses large language models to map literature-reported links among genetic variants, cancer types, and treatments at scale.
infographic.clinical_relevance: The tool may support precision oncology research and molecular tumour board preparation, but extracted associations do not establish treatment efficacy or suitability.
method: Screen biomedical abstracts for gene mentions.
Combine traditional NLP and LLMs to extract and standardise variant–treatment–cancer associations.
Use LLMs to verify associations against abstract text and build a searchable evidence graph.
infographic.evidence_signal: Of 886,195 eligible gene-containing abstracts, 37,895 mentioned all three entity types; LLM verification confirmed at least one association in 35,224 papers, yielding 44,644 verified graph edges.
infographic.watch_item: Abstract-based LLM verification is not independent clinical validation; extracted links require expert review before clinical interpretation.
infographic.paper_title: Variantscape: Retrospective Study of Large Language Model-Based Extraction of Variant-Treatment-Cancer Associations from Published Oncology Abstracts

title: Comprehensive real-world utilization, treatment trajectories, and outcomes of immune checkpoint inhibitors across cancer types: the multicenter FAIR-ICI cohort
authors: Ha, L. T.; Ver Donck, F.; Bassez, I.; Oeste, C. L.; Vulsteke, C.; Delombaerde, D.; Hens, D.; Prenen, H.; Croes, L.; De Meulenaere, A.; Debruyne, P. R.; Verhaert, M.; Aspeslagh, S.; Brusselaers, N.; Verbiest, A.
abstract: BackgroundImmune checkpoint inhibitors (ICIs) have transformed cancer treatment, yet evidence on their utilization, treatment trajectories, and effectiveness in routine clinical practice remains limited. We characterized real-world ICI use and outcomes across cancer types using the multicenter FAIR-ICI cohort and explored differences between real-world and pivotal trial outcomes. MethodsWe conducted a retrospective cohort study of adults receiving ICIs across four Belgian hospitals. Structured and unstructured electronic health record data were harmonized using the Observational Medical Outcomes Partnership Common Data Model (OMOP-CDM) and natural language processing. We evaluated overall survival (OS), time on treatment (ToT), time to next treatment (TTNT), ICI discontinuation (>12-week treatment gap without re-initiation), and post-discontinuation survival. OS was descriptively compared with pivotal trials, and prognostic factors were assessed using multivariable Cox regression. An interactive public dashboard was developed to enable exploration of cohort characteristics, treatment patterns, and outcomes. ResultsAmong 3,231 ICI-treated patients, 2,514 (77.8%) had metastatic disease. Among metastatic patients, 568 (22.6%) discontinued ICI without subsequent systemic therapy. Median post-discontinuation OS was 21.4 months (95% CI 16.5-37.2), with 49.1% alive at 24 months. ToT and TTNT were generally shorter than OS, particularly in melanoma (median OS 78 months; ToT 7 months; TTNT 26 months). Real-world survival was frequently less favorable than in pivotal trials. ECOG [≥]2 was associated with poorer OS than ECOG 0-1 (adjusted HR 2.18, 95% CI 1.82-2.60). In NSCLC patients receiving pembrolizumab plus chemotherapy, survival with ECOG 0-1 more closely approximated trial outcomes, whereas survival with ECOG [≥]2 was substantially poorer. ConclusionsReal-world ICI treatment trajectories extend beyond active treatment, with some patients experiencing prolonged survival after discontinuation. Differences between real-world and trial outcomes highlight the importance of patient characteristics, particularly performance status, when interpreting trial evidence in routine care. FAIR-ICI provides a scalable framework for evaluating real-world immunotherapy effectiveness, treatment trajectories, and future investigations of treatment-related toxicity. HighlightsO_LIFAIR-ICI studied 3,231 patients across four Belgian hospitals and provides an interactive dashboard for subgroup exploration. C_LIO_LIAmong metastatic patients, 22.6% stopped ICIs without subsequent systemic therapy, with 49.1% alive at 24 months after stopping. C_LIO_LITime on treatment and time to next treatment were generally shorter than overall survival. C_LIO_LIReal-world survival was frequently less favorable than in pivotal clinical trials. C_LIO_LIPoor ECOG performance status was strongly associated with shorter survival and may contribute to trial-real-world differences. C_LI

infographic.key_insight: In the FAIR-ICI real-world cohort, survival extended beyond active immunotherapy for some patients, while outcomes were frequently less favorable than in pivotal trials.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Performance status was strongly associated with survival, highlighting the importance of patient characteristics when interpreting trial results in routine cancer care.
method: Retrospective cohort of 3,231 adults receiving immune checkpoint inhibitors at four Belgian hospitals.
Harmonized electronic health records using OMOP-CDM and natural language processing.
Evaluated treatment trajectories and survival, with descriptive trial comparisons and multivariable Cox regression.
infographic.evidence_signal: Among 568 metastatic patients who discontinued immunotherapy without subsequent systemic therapy, median post-discontinuation survival was 21.4 months; ECOG ≥2 was associated with poorer overall survival than ECOG 0–1 (adjusted HR 2.18, 95% CI 1.82–2.60).
infographic.watch_item: This observational treatment-outcomes study—not an AI drug-discovery study—cannot establish that discontinuation causes prolonged survival, and trial comparisons were descriptive.
infographic.paper_title: Comprehensive real-world utilization, treatment trajectories, and outcomes of immune checkpoint inhibitors across cancer types: the multicenter FAIR-ICI cohort

title: Identifying interstitial lung disease with large language models on clinical notes and claims
authors: Larghero, G.; Schneeweiss, S.; Gu, B.; Anand, P.; Lin, J. K.; Yang, J.
abstract: BackgroundInterstitial lung disease (ILD) is a potentially fatal toxicity of immune check-point inhibitors and antibody-drug conjugates. Drug-safety studies in healthcare databases identify ILD with claims-based algorithms that trade positive predictive value (PPV) against sensitivity. We assessed whether large language models (LLMs) improve on these algorithms, with and without electronic health record (EHR) notes, and whether these gains translate into measurable epidemiological benefits. MethodsIn 309 oncology patients with ILD diagnosis codes at Mass General Brigham, adjudicated by two pulmonologists, we compared 12 open-access LLMs with 20 published claims-based algorithms. LLMs received claims, EHR notes, or both, without task-specific training. Measures were PPV and yield (proportion classified positive). We projected the attenuation of a drug-induced ILD odds ratio under non-differential outcome misclassification. FindingsLLMs extended the PPV-yield frontier of the published algorithms with all three inputs. Across the 36 model-input evaluations, LLM PPV exceeded that of the best algorithm without specialist-coding requirements (Algorithm 4) by 14.3 percentage points on average. With claims alone, Qwen3-8B achieved 89.8% PPV (95% CI 78.2-95.6) at 15.9% yield, versus 86.7% at 4.9% for the highest-PPV algorithm. With notes alone, Qwen3-32B achieved 78.9% PPV at 49.2% yield, versus 64.6% at 51.1% for Algorithm 4. With combined claims and notes, Qwen3-14B achieved 100.0% PPV at 24.3% yield. Under a simulated drug-safety scenario with a true odds ratio of 3.0, the projected observed odds ratio was 2.67 with combined inputs versus 1.07 with Algorithm 4, corresponding to a 46-fold difference in the estimated sample size required for 80% power (591 versus 27,200 patients). InterpretationZero-shot LLMs offer a higher-PPV alternative to rule-based claims pheno-typing for ILD, on all three input types. Because the claims-only configuration uses the same claims data as existing algorithms, it could be deployed in administrative databases without linked notes, and may recover drug-safety signal otherwise lost to outcome misclassification. FundingNational Institute on Aging, National Library of Medicine, PCORI, and the National Institute of Arthritis and Musculoskeletal and Skin Diseases. Research in contextO_ST_ABSEvidence before this studyC_ST_ABSWe searched PubMed up to August 2026 for studies on claims or electronic health record (EHR)-based identification of interstitial lung disease and on machine-learning or large language model (LLM) phenotyping of clinical conditions. Search terms included "interstitial lung disease or pneumonitis", "administrative claims", "computational phenotyping", "rule-based algorithms", "machine learning", and "large language models". We also screened the reference lists of relevant articles. The literature search suggested that identifying ILD in longitudinal claims data is unreliable because the relevant diagnosis codes are nonspecific, and validated rule-based algorithms face a structural tradeoff between PPV and coverage. Supervised machine-learning classifiers have outperformed rule-based ILD identification on electronic health record data, and zero-shot LLMs have already shown the ability to phenotype chronic conditions from structured codes. No study, however, had compared a zero-shot LLM head-to-head against validated, published claims-based algorithms for a specific, high-stakes drug-safety outcome on a single fixed cohort, isolated the contribution of the input substrate from that of the model, or quantified the downstream consequence for pharmacoepidemiologic effect estimation. Added value of this studyOn a single, fixed, expert-adjudicated cohort, the evaluated LLMs achieved higher positive predictive value (PPV) than all 20 published claims-based algorithms at comparable yield (the proportion of patients classified as ILD-positive), whether the models received structured claims, clinical notes, or both. Across the 36 model-input evaluations, PPV exceeded that of the most inclusive published rule by 19.7 percentage points on average, and did so in 33 of 36 evaluations. We show that clinical notes generally increased yield, while the resulting PPV-yield trade-off depended on the model and input combination. Restricting the input to a single EHR note type preserved the advantage over rule-based phenotyping in matched comparisons on the patients possessing that EHR note type. Most consequentially, this improvement reduces the sample size required to detect a hypothesised drug-ILD association from approximately 27,200 patients for the best existing algorithm for the task to 591 when using LLMs, and offer a deployable upgrade for the note-free administrative databases where rule-based algorithms are the current standard. Implications of all the available evidenceFor pharmacovigilance of treatment-related ILD, the limiting step is often not the size of the available claims database but the misclassification that erodes the very signal under surveillance. Replacing rule-based claims phenotyping algorithms with zero-shot LLM-based alternatives transforms a high-PPV, low-yield classifier into one that recovers many more patients at the same PPV, converting a classifier that can render drug-safety associations statistically invisible into one that makes them detectable in cohorts of feasible size. Pending external validation, this offers a practical route to more sensitive post-marketing surveillance of the pulmonary toxicity of immune checkpoint inhibitors and antibody-drug conjugates. More broadly, we hypothesise that this advantage is not specific to ILD: zero-shot LLM phenotyping may recover drug-safety signal for other outcomes that diagnosis codes capture poorly but that are well documented in clinical text, a possibility that warrants dedicated evaluation.

infographic.key_insight: Zero-shot large language models improved the positive predictive value–yield trade-off for identifying interstitial lung disease (ILD) compared with published claims-based algorithms.
infographic.clinical_relevance: More accurate ILD identification could strengthen cancer-drug safety studies by reducing outcome misclassification and preserving toxicity signals.
method: Evaluated 12 open-access LLMs using claims, clinical notes, or both, without task-specific training.
Compared performance with 20 published claims-based algorithms using positive predictive value (PPV) and yield.
Projected effects of outcome misclassification on drug-safety odds ratios and study sample sizes.
infographic.evidence_signal: Among 309 oncology patients with ILD diagnosis codes and pulmonologist-adjudicated outcomes, claims-only Qwen3-8B achieved 89.8% PPV at 15.9% yield, versus 86.7% PPV at 4.9% yield for the highest-PPV algorithm.
infographic.watch_item: Validation beyond this single-health-system, diagnosis-code-selected cohort is needed; projected drug-safety benefits were simulated, not demonstrated in a prospective study.
infographic.paper_title: Identifying interstitial lung disease with large language models on clinical notes and claims

title: Enhancing deep sleep with auditory stimulation to boost cognitive training responsiveness in people with Parkinson's disease and mild cognitive impairment: Rationale and design of the double-blind randomized controlled trial PD-CogT-Sleep
authors: Ophey, A.; Kleinsorge, M. T.; Wallimann, N. A.; Maric, A.; Loosli, S. V.; Mollenhauer, B.; Balint, B.; Huber, R.; Baumann, C. R.; Kalbe, E.; Schreiner, S. J.
abstract: BackgroundCognitive training (CogT) is an established non-pharmacological intervention for people with Parkinsons disease (PD) and mild cognitive impairment (PD-MCI). However, overall effects on cognitive outcomes are small to moderate and interindividually highly heterogeneous. Sleep -especially deep sleep-could be an important determinant of CogT responsiveness in PD, and may have beneficial effects on PD pathophysiology. Therefore, the enhancement of deep sleep by phase-targeted auditory stimulation (PTAS) could strengthen the effects of CogT on cognitive symptoms and counteract disease progression. MethodsPD-CogT-Sleep is a monocentric, partly decentralized, double-blind, randomized sham-controlled trial that combines two remotely delivered non-pharmacological interventions, to assess the additive effect of PTAS on digital CogT responsiveness in people with PD-MCI. The primary outcome is executive functions; Secondary and exploratory outcomes include further cognitive functions, participant-reported outcome measures, blood-based biomarkers, and high-density sleep electroencephalography markers. Outcomes are assessed at baseline, five weeks post-allocation and at 3-month follow-up. We aim to consecutively recruit N=50 participants, who will be randomized 1:1 to receive CogT+PTAS or CogT+Sham. DiscussionThe PD-CogT-Sleep study integrates wearable and digital technologies to systematically combine a novel, non-invasive, sleep-enhancing intervention (PTAS) with established CogT to improve cognition and evaluate PTAS disease-modifying potential through its effects on blood-based biomarkers in PD-MCI. The expected results will foster our understanding of the interplay of sleep, cognition, and neurodegeneration, and may guide further development of safe, feasible, scalable, patient-centered, technology-based non-pharmacological interventions counteracting cognitive decline in neurodegenerative diseases. infographic.key_insight: PD-CogT-Sleep will test whether auditory stimulation targeting deep sleep improves cognitive training responsiveness in people with Parkinson’s disease and mild cognitive impairment.
infographic.clinical_relevance: If effective, this non-pharmacological combination could help address cognitive difficulties in Parkinson’s disease, but benefits remain unproven.
method: Single-center, double-blind, randomized sham-controlled trial targeting 50 participants.
Compare remotely delivered digital cognitive training plus phase-targeted auditory stimulation versus training plus sham stimulation.
Assess outcomes at baseline, five weeks post-allocation, and three-month follow-up.
infographic.evidence_signal: This design paper reports no efficacy results; planned assessments prioritize executive function and include other cognitive outcomes, participant reports, blood biomarkers, and sleep EEG markers.

title: AI-Based MRI Radiomics for Preoperative Detection of Tumor Deposits in Rectal Cancer: A Bivariate Diagnostic Accuracy Meta-analysis
authors: Alsaied, M. A.; Hegazy, M.; Saleh, M. M.; Barakat, B.; Ibrahim, O. R.; Abdelrazek, H. M.; Nazemi, S.; El-Hussuna, A.; Shalaby, M.
abstract: Background: In rectal cancer (RC), tumor deposits (TDs) are clinically important as they are associated with a negative impact on prognosis and affect risk stratification as well as management plans. MRI radiomics combined with artificial intelligence (AI) has been explored for non-invasive preoperative TDs detection. However, results vary across studies; therefore, we performed a systematic review and meta-analysis to pool their diagnostic test accuracy (DTA). Methods: This systematic review and DTA meta-analysis were conducted in accordance with the Cochrane Handbook for Systematic Reviews of Diagnostic Test Accuracy and reported in adherence to the Preferred Reporting Items for Systematic Reviews and Meta-Analyses of Diagnostic Test Accuracy Studies (PRISMA-DTA). Databases were screened for DTA studies of MRI-based radiomics predicting TDs in adult RC patients with histopathology as reference. Results: Nine studies (2589 patients) were identified. Across included studies, the bivariate meta-analysis showed pooled sensitivity of 0.765 (95% CI 0.714 - 0.809) and specificity of 0.790 (95% CI 0.750 - 0.825), with overall AUC of 0.845 and very low heterogeneity (I2 = 7.3%). In validation datasets, diagnostic performance remained consistent (AUC 0.806), with pooled sensitivity 0.751 (95% CI 0.681 - 0.809) and specificity 0.751 (95% CI 0.681 - 0.809). For MRI modality, T2 weighted image (T2WI) showed higher sensitivity (0.745) than T2WI plus diffusion weighted image (DWI) (0.697), while T2WI+DWI had higher specificity (0.809 vs 0.737) and AUC (0.829 vs 0.796), with no significant subgroup differences (p[≥]0.192). Models combining radiomics with clinical/radiological variables achieved significantly higher sensitivity (0.842 vs 0.657, p<0.001) and higher AUC (0.827 vs 0.752), with comparable specificity. Conclusion: MRI-based radiomics demonstrates good accuracy for preoperative detection of tumor deposits in RC. The integration of radiomics with clinical or imaging features increases the accuracy of identification. Amongst the MRI modalities, models that utilize the combination of T2WI plus DWI are more accurate than those using T2WI or DWI only.

infographic.key_insight: AI-based MRI radiomics showed good accuracy for preoperative detection of tumor deposits in rectal cancer, with pooled sensitivity of 76.5% and specificity of 79.0%.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Detecting tumor deposits before surgery could inform risk stratification, although these findings do not establish readiness for routine clinical use.
method: Systematic review and bivariate diagnostic accuracy meta-analysis.
Evaluated MRI radiomics against histopathology in adults with rectal cancer.
Compared MRI sequences and radiomics-only versus combined clinical/radiological models.
infographic.evidence_signal: Across 9 studies involving 2,589 patients, pooled AUC was 0.845 and validation-dataset AUC was 0.806; combined models had higher sensitivity than radiomics alone (84.2% vs 65.7%, p<0.001).
infographic.watch_item: MRI-sequence subgroup differences were not statistically significant, so superiority of T2WI plus DWI remains uncertain.
infographic.paper_title: AI-Based MRI Radiomics for Preoperative Detection of Tumor Deposits in Rectal Cancer: A Bivariate Diagnostic Accuracy Meta-analysis

title: Alzheimers disease and psychiatric polygenic risk are disease-specific and independent of plasma biomarkers in a real-world young-onset dementia cohort.
authors: Bhalala, O. G.; Longfei, W.; Gerring, Z. F.; Han, J.; Kang, M. J.; Trounson, B. O.; Loi, S. M.; Velakoulis, D.; Eratne, D.; Bahlo, M.; The MiND Study Group,
abstract: BackgroundYoung-onset dementia is frequently misdiagnosed, particularly where neurodegenerative and primary psychiatric disorders (PPD) overlap. Plasma biomarkers measure current pathology, whereas polygenic risk scores (PRS) capture lifelong genetic risk. Whether PRS derived from late-onset and population samples transfer to young-onset presentations, and how they relate to plasma biomarkers, is unknown. MethodsWe studied 687 participants of European ancestry from the Markers in Neuropsychiatric Disorders (MiND) Study, a prospective young-onset neuropsychiatry cohort: 195 healthy controls (HC), 283 PPD, 55 Alzheimers disease (AD) and 154 non-AD neurodegenerative disease (oNDG). PRS for AD, a cross-disorder psychiatric factor (PSY), frontotemporal dementia, Lewy body dementia and Parkinsons disease were computed with PRS-CS, excluding the APOE locus. Plasma NfL, GFAP and p-tau217 were available for 332 participants. Models were adjusted for age, sex and APOE {varepsilon}4 dose. ResultsRelative to HC, the AD PRS was associated with AD (OR 1.69 per SD, 95% CI 1.17- 2.45) but not PPD (0.95, 0.77-1.16). The PSY PRS showed the reciprocal pattern (PPD 1.29, 1.05-1.58; AD 1.00, 0.72-1.40). No PRS was associated with any plasma protein. In distinguishing PPD from oNDG, NfL was the strongest discriminator (OR 2.15, 1.62-2.83). The AD PRS was also associated with oNDG (1.38, 1.11-1.71), without improving discrimination (AUC 0.764 for NfL alone versus 0.773 combined). ConclusionIn young-onset presentations, AD and psychiatric polygenic risk are disease-specific and independent of plasma biomarkers of neurodegeneration. Their combined diagnostic value requires evaluation in larger, longitudinal pre-clinical cohorts.

infographic.key_insight: In a young-onset neuropsychiatry cohort, Alzheimer’s and psychiatric polygenic risk scores showed distinct disease associations, with no detected associations with plasma biomarkers.
infographic.clinical_relevance: Genetic risk and plasma biomarkers may capture different information, but their combined diagnostic value remains unproven.
method: Studied 687 European-ancestry participants: 195 controls, 283 with primary psychiatric disorders, 55 with Alzheimer’s disease and 154 with other neurodegenerative diseases.
Computed five polygenic risk scores excluding APOE; adjusted models for age, sex and APOE ε4 dose.
Evaluated plasma NfL, GFAP and p-tau217 in 332 participants.
infographic.evidence_signal: Alzheimer’s and psychiatric risk scores were associated with their corresponding diagnoses versus controls (OR per SD 1.69 and 1.29, respectively); adding Alzheimer’s genetic risk to NfL yielded little change in psychiatric-versus-other-neurodegenerative discrimination (AUC 0.764 to 0.773).
infographic.watch_item: The European-ancestry sample and small Alzheimer’s subgroup limit generalizability; larger longitudinal cohorts are needed before clinical implementation.
infographic.paper_title: Alzheimers disease and psychiatric polygenic risk are disease-specific and independent of plasma biomarkers in a real-world young-onset dementia cohort.
